chapters.title: Romans 1 — The gospel, God’s righteousness, and the need for grace
chapters.historicalContext: Paul introduces himself as an apostle set apart for the gospel concerning Jesus, then addresses believers in Rome, a community likely made up of Jewish and Gentile followers. He describes the gospel as God’s power for salvation and begins a difficult account of humanity’s rejection of God.
chapters.overview: The chapter introduces the letter’s central theme: God’s righteousness is revealed through the gospel and received by faith. Paul then describes the disorder that follows when people exchange the Creator for created things.
chapters.studyObservation: Paul’s opening connects Jesus with Israel’s Scriptures and the promised Davidic line. The description of idolatry and human disorder prepares for the argument about universal need and the danger of judging others.
chapters.connectionNotes: Read Romans 1 with the argument that follows in chapters 2–3. Paul’s description of human failure is not permission for readers to place themselves above others; the letter soon turns the critique toward every person.
chapters.lifeApplication: Receive the gospel as good news rather than a basis for superiority. Honour the Creator, examine the things that compete for ultimate loyalty, and approach others with humility.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: The vice list and discussion of human disorder must not be used to single out one group as uniquely sinful or to justify contempt, harassment, or dehumanisation. Paul’s argument moves toward the need for grace for all.
chapters.readingNote: Follow Paul’s greeting and his statement about the gospel before reading the description of humanity’s disorder. Keep the whole letter’s argument in view, especially the impartial judgement developed in chapter 2.
studyQuestions: How does Paul describe the gospel and its power?
What does the exchange of Creator for created things reveal about idolatry?
Why should chapter 1 be read alongside Paul’s argument in chapter 2?

chapters.title: Romans 2 — God’s impartial judgement and the danger of hypocrisy
chapters.historicalContext: Paul addresses the person who judges others while practising similar wrongdoing. He argues that God judges impartially, considers both those with and without the law, and examines what circumcision and covenant identity mean when they are not matched by faithfulness.
chapters.overview: The chapter turns the moral critique back on the reader. Possessing the law or a visible religious identity does not exempt anyone from judgement; God looks at truth and the reality of the heart.
chapters.studyObservation: Paul speaks within Jewish scriptural traditions about divine justice and covenant faithfulness. His argument challenges hypocrisy and privilege rather than dismissing the law or Jewish identity.
chapters.connectionNotes: Romans 2 is part of Paul’s case that all people need grace. It must not be separated from Romans 3 or used to claim that Jewish people are uniquely hypocritical.
chapters.lifeApplication: Examine your own conduct before judging others. Let religious knowledge lead to humility, integrity, and practical goodness rather than status or condemnation.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: The chapter does not teach that people earn salvation by moral performance. Paul is exposing hypocrisy and impartial judgement; do not use it to attack Jewish communities or any other group.
chapters.readingNote: Notice how Paul shifts from describing wrongdoing to addressing the person who judges. The chapter prepares the conclusion that no group can claim exemption from God’s impartial assessment.
studyQuestions: Why does Paul challenge the person who judges others?
What does impartial judgement mean in this chapter?
How does Paul distinguish outward religious identity from faithfulness of the heart?

chapters.title: Romans 3 — All are accountable and righteousness comes through faith
chapters.historicalContext: Paul concludes that both Jews and Gentiles are under sin, while affirming the value of Israel’s Scriptures. He then presents God’s righteousness revealed apart from works of the law and received through faith in Jesus, with grace and redemption at the centre.
chapters.overview: The chapter establishes universal need and the gift of justification. No group can boast, because all have sinned and are put right through God’s grace rather than through human achievement.
chapters.studyObservation: Paul strings together scriptural quotations to show the reach of human wrongdoing. The law exposes sin, while the language of redemption and sacrifice explains how God acts to restore people.
chapters.connectionNotes: Paul’s argument does not erase the gifts entrusted to Israel or imply that Jewish people are worse than Gentiles. The letter’s emphasis is that both groups stand in need of grace.
chapters.lifeApplication: Let grace remove boasting and create gratitude. Treat others as people who need the same mercy, and allow faith to produce humility and justice rather than superiority.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: The phrase ‘all have sinned’ must not be used to shame people who are already burdened or to excuse harmful behaviour. Justification by grace does not remove the call to accountability and changed living.
chapters.readingNote: Read the conclusion about universal sin before the section on justification. Paul’s movement is from shared accountability to God’s gracious action, which excludes boasting and opens the way for reconciliation.
studyQuestions: What advantages does Paul still recognise in Israel’s Scriptures and calling?
How does the law expose sin without becoming the means of justification?
Why does grace leave no room for boasting?

chapters.title: Romans 4 — Abraham, faith, and the promise that includes the nations
chapters.historicalContext: Paul uses Abraham and David to show that righteousness is credited through faith rather than earned by works. Abraham’s faith precedes circumcision, and the promise rests on God’s power to give life and fulfil what has been spoken.
chapters.overview: The chapter places faith at the heart of God’s promise and shows that Abraham can be the father of all who trust God, circumcised or uncircumcised. The promise depends on grace, not human achievement.
chapters.studyObservation: Paul reads Genesis and the Psalms as witnesses to faith and forgiveness. Abraham’s trust is not presented as flawless confidence but as reliance on the God who gives life to the dead.
chapters.connectionNotes: Paul’s reading of Abraham is an argument within Jewish Scripture, not a rejection of Jewish heritage. The promise to Abraham is widened to include the nations without erasing its origins.
chapters.lifeApplication: Trust God’s faithfulness even when circumstances seem uncertain. Welcome others as fellow recipients of grace and resist using religious practices as badges of superiority.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Faith is not a technique for guaranteeing every desired outcome. Abraham’s story should not be used to blame people whose hopes are delayed or whose circumstances remain difficult.
chapters.readingNote: Follow Paul’s use of Abraham before and after circumcision, then notice how David’s words about forgiveness support the same point. The chapter presents promise as grounded in God’s faithfulness.
studyQuestions: Why does Paul emphasise that Abraham was counted righteous before circumcision?
How does grace change the meaning of the promise?
What does Abraham’s trust teach about hoping when circumstances seem impossible?

chapters.title: Romans 5 — Peace with God, hope in suffering, and Adam and Christ
chapters.historicalContext: Paul describes the results of justification: peace with God, access to grace, hope, and love poured out through the Spirit. He then contrasts Adam’s trespass with Christ’s gift, presenting Jesus’ obedience as the source of life and grace.
chapters.overview: The chapter moves from justification to its consequences in a transformed relationship with God. Suffering is not celebrated, but hope is sustained by God’s love; the Adam-Christ contrast shows grace overcoming the reach of sin and death.
chapters.studyObservation: Paul describes a sequence from suffering to endurance and hope, grounded in the Spirit’s gift. The comparison of Adam and Christ frames the scope of the human problem and the greater reach of grace.
chapters.connectionNotes: The teaching about suffering should not be used to tell people that harm is good or that they should remain in unsafe situations. Interpret the Adam-Christ comparison with attention to the gift and abundance of grace.
chapters.lifeApplication: Receive peace as a gift, support people who suffer, and let hope produce patient love. Practise gratitude for grace that is greater than human failure.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Do not romanticise trauma or claim that every painful event is sent to improve someone. Paul’s confidence is in God’s love within suffering, not in suffering as a good in itself.
chapters.readingNote: Read the opening section as the outcome of justification, then follow the Adam-Christ comparison. Notice how Paul repeatedly emphasises the abundance of grace over the power of sin.
studyQuestions: What results of justification does Paul name?
How does hope remain grounded when people suffer?
What contrast does Paul draw between Adam’s trespass and Christ’s gift?

chapters.title: Romans 6 — United with Christ and freed to live a new life
chapters.historicalContext: Paul answers the idea that grace might encourage continued sin. Through baptism, believers are described as united with Christ in his death and resurrection, freed from sin’s mastery, and called to offer themselves to God as instruments of righteousness.
chapters.overview: Grace does not make wrongdoing irrelevant; it opens a new way of life. Believers are no longer to treat sin as their master but to live from the new identity given through Christ.
chapters.studyObservation: The slavery imagery contrasts two forms of allegiance and their outcomes. Paul’s point is liberation from sin’s rule, not permission for human beings to enslave or dominate one another.
chapters.connectionNotes: The baptism language is interpreted differently across Christian traditions, but the chapter’s ethical direction is clear: union with Christ calls for changed conduct. Do not confuse struggle with the absence of grace.
chapters.lifeApplication: Practise habits that reflect your new allegiance: truthfulness, self-control, justice, and care. Seek support when old patterns are difficult to change, and remember that growth is lived over time.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Paul’s slavery metaphor must never be used to justify human slavery, coercion, or abusive control. The chapter does not teach that a person who struggles has been abandoned by God.
chapters.readingNote: Follow Paul’s question about continuing in sin with the baptism imagery and the contrast between masters. The chapter links grace with a new identity and a new pattern of living.
studyQuestions: Why does Paul reject the idea that grace permits continued wrongdoing?
What does being united with Christ in baptism signify?
How does the slavery metaphor describe a change of allegiance without justifying human domination?

chapters.title: Romans 7 — The law, the struggle with sin, and the need for deliverance
chapters.historicalContext: Paul uses the analogy of marriage and death to explain a changed relationship to the law through Christ. He then discusses the law’s goodness and the conflict experienced when people know what is right but find themselves drawn toward wrongdoing.
chapters.overview: The chapter distinguishes the goodness of the law from sin’s power to distort human desire. The struggle reveals the need for deliverance beyond willpower and prepares for the Spirit-led life in chapter 8.
chapters.studyObservation: Paul’s first-person description has been interpreted as autobiographical, representative, or both. Whatever the reading, the passage names the frustration of divided desire and the limits of self-reliance.
chapters.connectionNotes: Do not use the struggle described here to excuse harmful behaviour or to tell people that change is impossible. The chapter’s question leads toward deliverance and life in the Spirit, not resignation.
chapters.lifeApplication: Acknowledge struggle honestly, seek help and accountability, and do not rely on willpower alone. Let the desire to do good lead toward dependence on God and practical steps of change.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: The passage is not a diagnosis of every mental or emotional struggle, nor does it mean people are powerless to make responsible choices. Avoid shaming people who experience recurring difficulties.
chapters.readingNote: Read the section on the law’s purpose before the first-person struggle. Notice the final cry for deliverance and how it prepares the transition to the assurance of Romans 8.
studyQuestions: How does Paul distinguish the law from the power of sin?
What does the divided desire in the chapter reveal about human limitation?
How does the final cry for deliverance prepare for Romans 8?

chapters.title: Romans 8 — Life in the Spirit, hope in suffering, and God’s enduring love
chapters.historicalContext: Paul declares there is no condemnation for those in Christ and describes life led by the Spirit. He speaks of adoption, the groaning of creation, hope amid suffering, the Spirit’s help in prayer, and the assurance that nothing can separate believers from God’s love in Christ.
chapters.overview: The chapter brings together freedom, adoption, hope, and assurance. The Spirit gives life and helps in weakness, while the whole creation waits for renewal and believers are held by God’s love.
chapters.studyObservation: Paul’s language of adoption gives believers a new identity and inheritance. The groaning of creation and the Spirit’s intercession acknowledge suffering rather than denying it, and the closing assurance rests on God’s action in Christ.
chapters.connectionNotes: The promise that all things work together for good should not be used to call evil good or to silence grief. Paul’s assurance is that suffering cannot separate people from God’s love, not that every event is beneficial in itself.
chapters.lifeApplication: Live from the assurance of God’s love, care for creation, and support people who suffer. When words fail in prayer, trust that the Spirit helps in weakness and remain open to hope.
chapters.interpretiveCaution: Do not use Romans 8 to shame people who grieve, experience anxiety, or cannot see a positive outcome. The passage does not guarantee freedom from hardship or promise that every believer will receive the same earthly result.
chapters.readingNote: Follow the movement from no condemnation to life in the Spirit, then to creation’s groaning and the closing assurance. Notice how hope and honest recognition of suffering are held together.
studyQuestions: What does life in the Spirit mean in contrast with life governed by sin?
How does Paul describe creation’s groaning and the Spirit’s help?
What does the closing passage promise, and what does it not promise about suffering?
